newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank, Bonn on warpath to cap dollar gains.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank, Bonn on warpath to cap dollar gains.

text.p: Germany's powerful Bundesbank and the Bonn finance ministry on Wednesday issued a two-pronged attack on a surging dollar, acting to counter a report that Germany was keen to see the U.S. currency move still higher.

Chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber, in an official statement from the central bank, said the Bundesbank continued to support a statement made by the Group of Seven industrial nations at a meeting in Berlin this weekend.
"That statement said the dollar has been corrected, and it was made at a rate of 1.65 marks," he said.
"We have nothing to add to the G7 statement," a finance ministry spokesman said.

The dollar, which had surged to about 1.69 marks on a report from Market News Service saying Germany would welcome a further rise in the dollar, fell to as low as 1.6750 marks in an immediate response to the Bundesbank comments.
But the dramatic impact was short-lived. The U.S. currency then crept back to above 1.68 marks in morning trade and had recovered to trade as high as 1.6860 by 1230 GMT.

Market News Service, quoting sources close to the German finance ministry and central bank, had reported on Tuesday that Germany would welcome a further rise in the dollar to a range of 1.70 to 1.75 marks over time to boost its economy.

The report came hot on the heels of statement from the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- which welcomed the strong dollar but carefully avoided giving the currency a push in either direction.
"We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets, noted in our April 1995 communique, have been corrected," a brief statement issued after the G7 meeting said.

"We reaffirmed our views that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility is undesirable. We agreed to monitor developments on the currency markets and to coooperate as appropriate," the statement added.
Both the Bundesbank and the finance ministry in Bonn made clear on Wednesday that they stuck by the Berlin statement.
But the Bundesbank statement went further in denying that it shared the views expressed in the MNSI report.

"The Bundesbank firmly backs the Berlin statement. The Bundesbank is definitively not of the opinion that the dollar should rise further," Koerber said. "The opinion expressed in the MNSI report does not exist within the Bundesbank."

In Paris, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said the dollar's rise reflected fundamentals, but added "it is necessary for the new situation to consolidate and that we avoid volatility, that is to say that there is stability."

Despite apparent discord in advance of the G7 meeting -- with Japan and Germany apparently seeking to brake the dollar but the United States and France content to see further gains -- once in Berlin the officials spoke as with one voice.

Comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin -- who said a strong dollar was in U.S. interests but simultaneously noted it had been strong for some time now -- set the tone for a series of calls for the dollar to stabilise at its new level.
The dollar's response to the G7 statement when markets reopened on Monday was moderate, trending slightly lower.

Demonstrating his satisfaction with that response, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, speaking in Basle in Switzerland on Monday, said the markets had so far acted in "an appropriate way" to the G7's message.
Only two years ago the G7 acted to bring the dollar back from record lows against the mark and yen by calling for its orderly reversal.
Its rise has been particularly good for Europe, boosting exports and lifting growth as countries rush to cut budget deficits in time for the launch of a single currency in 1999.

It has also helped the United States, keeping import prices low and helping to maintain low inflation in its own economy, though U.S. carmakers are beginning to squeal about the effect of the dollar's rise on their exports.
But the dollar's gains have forced sharp losses for the yen, which is starting to threaten Japan's financial system.

Analysts are also concerned that a persistent slide in the usually robust German mark could lead to inflationary problems in Germany and give Europe a weak anchor currency at a critical moment in the transition to the European single currency.
"The Bundesbank is trying to cap the rise of the dollar. What the bank is concerned about is the speed with which the currency is rising," said Armin Kayser at SBC Warburg.
"If it overshoots it could create problems for stability with import prices," he added.
